For the first time ever, a robot has built a structure in space, without a single astronaut.
It's called ASTRA, made at Caltech. It launched on March thirtieth, packed in a box about one cubic metre in size.
Why build up there? Because rockets are narrow. The Webb telescope's six and a half metre mirror had to fold up like origami just to fit.
ASTRA does it differently. Its robotic arm takes struts and joints from dispensers, and puts together one box-shaped bay.
It stretches a shiny net across it, pushes the bay out into space, and starts the next one.
The target: an antenna dish one point four metres wide, made of eleven bays. Time ran short. It finished three.
Small? Sure. But the goal is structures hundreds of metres, even kilometres, wide.
So the giant telescopes of tomorrow may never ride a rocket in one piece. Robots will build them in orbit.
